Moralistic Therapeutic Deism (MTD)
muh-RAL-is-tik thair-uh-PYOO-tik DEE-iz-um
noun phrase (sociological-theological category)
Term coined by sociologist Christian Smith and Melinda Lundquist Denton in Soul Searching: The Religious and Spiritual Lives of American Teenagers (Oxford, 2005) to describe the de facto religion of American adolescents as revealed in the National Study of Youth and Religion (2001-2005). The label has since become the standard sociological-theological term for the religion of much of contemporary American Christianity, not just adolescents.

📖 Biblical Definition

Moralistic Therapeutic Deism (MTD) is the de facto religion of much of contemporary American Christianity, named by Christian Smith from the 2001-2005 National Study of Youth and Religion. Smith summarized its five tenets: (1) a God exists who created the world and watches over human life; (2) God wants people to be good, nice, and fair to each other, as taught in the Bible and most world religions; (3) the central goal of life is to be happy and feel good about oneself; (4) God is not particularly involved in one's life except when needed to resolve a problem; (5) good people go to heaven when they die. As Smith observed, this is not historic Christianity. It is a deistic background-God plus therapeutic self-actualization plus a vague moralism, with no place for sin, the cross, the Spirit, the church, the second coming, or any of the doctrinal substance of Reformed-confessional Christianity. The label MTD became immediately useful because Smith documented that it had displaced historic Christianity as the operative religion of most American Protestant teenagers (and, by extension, the operative religion of much of seeker-sensitive American Evangelicalism that shaped them). The Reformed reader receives MTD as a thorough diagnosis: the contemporary therapeutic register has substituted for the gospel and must be replaced by recovered Reformed-confessional Christianity. # voice-lock-ok: therapy: this entry uses 'therapeutic' to describe the corruption pattern Smith named.

MORALISTIC THERAPEUTIC DEISM, noun phrase. Coined by Christian Smith and Melinda Lundquist Denton, Soul Searching (2005).

Five tenets: (1) creator God watching over life; (2) God wants people to be good; (3) life's goal is happiness and self-esteem; (4) God minimally involved except in crisis; (5) good people go to heaven.

Not historic Christianity. Diagnosed as the operative religion of most contemporary American Protestant teenagers and (by extension) much of the seeker-sensitive Evangelical movement that shaped them.

Standard sociological-theological label for the religion-of-contemporary-American-Christianity in serious diagnostic literature.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

MTD is itself the corruption pattern being named. The entry exists to identify the five-point diagnosis as Smith offered it, document its displacement of historic Christianity, and prescribe Reformed-confessional recovery.

expand to see more

Substitution for historic Christianity. MTD shares vocabulary with Christianity (God, Bible, heaven, prayer) but has substituted radically different content. The God of MTD is deistic and uninvolved (not the LORD of covenant who speaks, redeems, judges, dwells). The Bible of MTD is moral advice (not the inspired, inerrant Word that pierces to dividing soul and spirit, Heb 4:12). Heaven in MTD is the destination of good people (not the eternal communion of those who have been washed in the blood of the Lamb). The substitution is so thorough that an entire generation of American Protestant teenagers grew up assuming MTD was Christianity; the recovery requires explicit Reformed-confessional teaching, not vague spirituality.

Therapeutic register substitution. MTD's third tenet — the central goal of life is to be happy and feel good about oneself — is the displacement of the Westminster Shorter Catechism's first answer: man's chief end is to glorify God and to enjoy him forever. The two answers are not complementary; they are competing summaries of human telos. Reformed-confessional recovery from MTD requires recovering the doxological-doctrinal frame in which the soul's true peace and joy are found in the worship of God, not in the affirmation of the self. # voice-lock-ok: therapy: 'therapeutic register' is named here as the corruption pattern.
